chapter.name: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice

questions.q: A family has to cut Rs 2,000 from its monthly spending and the members list four possible cuts. Using the chapter's examples of needs and wants, which cut leaves every need untouched?
questions.a: Dropping the planned holiday trip
o: Dropping the planned holiday trip
Buying less grain and pulses
Stopping the payment for a rented room
Reducing the family's drinking-water supply

questions.q: A school library has 5 copies of a new storybook and 20 students want to read it. Which feature of this situation makes it an economic problem rather than an ordinary dispute?
questions.a: Wants for the book exceed the copies, so a choice must be made
o: Wants for the book exceed the copies, so a choice must be made
The storybook is an essential like food, so the school must supply every one of the 20 students at once
Libraries are physical markets, so prices alone decide who gets the book first
The 5 copies can be put to only one use, so no choice is involved at all

questions.q: A company has a stock of steel. It can make refrigerator bodies, medical equipment or aircraft parts, but the stock is not enough for all three. Which pair of features of resources does this show?
questions.a: Limited in quantity and open to many alternative uses
o: Limited in quantity and open to many alternative uses
Unlimited in quantity and fit for only a single use
Limited in quantity and fit for only a single use
Unlimited in quantity and open to many alternative uses

questions.q: At 12 Arjun wanted a bicycle, at 16 a motorbike and at 25 a car. Which conclusion matches the chapter's account of wants?
questions.a: Wants keep changing, so satisfying one does not bring wants to an end
o: Wants keep changing, so satisfying one does not bring wants to an end
Wants stop once a person owns a car, because the car is the last want
Bicycles are needs and cars are wants, so his wants changed category
His resources grew with each want, so scarcity disappeared

questions.q: Twenty students want a storybook and the library has 5 copies, so 15 students must wait. This mismatch between unlimited wants and limited resources is called ___.
questions.a: scarcity

questions.q: Shreya orders a notebook through a shopping website and the seller delivers it. Using the chapter's description of a market, how should her purchase be described?
questions.a: It was a virtual market, as a market can be online
o: It was a virtual market, as a market can be online
It took place outside any market, since a market must be a physical place only
It was a government purchase, since only the state can run a market online
It was a need, so it cannot belong to any market in the chapter's sense

questions.q:
Read the statements about needs, wants and resources.
I. Needs are essentials such as food, water and shelter, while gadgets, vacations and luxury items are wants.
II. Once basic needs are met, human wants stop changing and scarcity disappears.
III. Natural and human-made resources are limited in quantity and can be used in many alternative ways.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I only
II only
I and II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Individuals, enterprises and governments all have to make economic choices.
Reason (R): Resources are limited in quantity and have alternative uses, while human wants are unlimited.
Choose the correct alternative.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true

questions.q:
A family's monthly income is Rs 9,000. It spends Rs 5,400 on food, water and rent, Rs 2,700 on a gadget upgrade and a holiday, and saves the rest.
(a) What percentage of the income goes to needs?
(b) Income falls to Rs 7,200 while the spending on needs stays the same. How much is left for wants and savings together, and what does this show about wants and resources?
questions.a: (a) 5400/9000 x 100 = 60 per cent. (b) 7,200 - 5,400 = Rs 1,800, so fewer wants can be met than before. Wants stay unlimited while the resources available to meet them are limited.
s: (a) 60 per cent from 5,400 out of 9,000
(b) Rs 1,800 left and the link to unlimited wants against limited resources

questions.q: True or False: When a person has enough food, water and shelter, her wants are also fully satisfied. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Food, water and shelter are needs; wants such as gadgets and vacations are separate and unlimited, and they keep changing, so meeting needs does not end wants.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: needs and wants are different, and wants are unlimited and keep changing

questions.q: Differentiate between a need and a want, and give one example of each from a student's school week.
questions.a: A need is an essential such as food, water or shelter (e.g. lunch); a want is something like a gadget, a vacation or a luxury item (e.g. a new gaming console).
s: Need and want correctly differentiated
One suitable example of each

questions.q:
A workshop has 12 tonnes of steel. It uses 5 tonnes for medical equipment and 4 tonnes for refrigerators.
(a) How many tonnes remain?
(b) The remaining tonnes can go to aircraft parts or to more refrigerators. In the chapter's terms, why is this an economic choice?
questions.a: (a) 12 - 5 - 4 = 3 tonnes. (b) Steel is a limited resource with alternative uses, so choosing one use means the other is given up.
s: (a) 3 tonnes
(b) Limited resource, alternative uses, one given up when the other is chosen

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why all human wants can never be satisfied.
questions.a: Human wants are unlimited and keep changing (a bicycle leads to a motorbike and then a car), whereas the resources needed to meet them are limited in quantity.
s: Wants are unlimited and keep changing
Resources are limited

questions.q: Neha says, 'Scarcity is a problem only for poor families. A rich family or a rich country never has to make economic choices.' Examine her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No, the claim fails. The chapter says individuals, enterprises and governments all face choices because wants are unlimited and resources, even a nation's, are limited with alternative uses. A government must still choose between highways and hospitals.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: unlimited wants against limited resources at every level
A chapter example showing a government or enterprise choosing

questions.q: Write a short situation of your own in which a government has two competing uses for one resource and cannot do both. Name the resource, the two uses and say what is given up.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. a state has a fixed sum of money (resource) for building a highway or for a hospital; if it builds the highway, the hospital is given up.
s: A believable situation with the resource named
Two competing uses identified
What is given up when one is chosen

questions.q: The school library has 5 copies and 20 students want the book. Explain why both 'let the students share' and 'buy more copies' are economic choices.
questions.a: Both are ways of dealing with limited copies against unlimited wants. Sharing uses the existing copies among more readers, while buying more uses the school's limited money, which has other uses and so has an opportunity cost.
s: The gap between wants and the 5 copies is scarcity
Sharing is a choice about using existing resources
Buying uses limited money with alternative uses

questions.q:
A town council has Rs 40 lakh. A new road costs Rs 25 lakh and a hospital wing costs Rs 22 lakh.
(i) Show by calculation that the council cannot fund both.
(ii) Name the resource, its alternative uses and what is given up if the road is chosen.
(iii) Give one consideration for each choice and say which you would choose, with a reason.
questions.a: (i) 25 + 22 = Rs 47 lakh, which is Rs 7 lakh more than the Rs 40 lakh available. (ii) The resource is the council's money; its uses are the road and the hospital wing; choosing the road gives up the hospital wing. (iii) The road helps movement and trade; the wing serves health needs. Any choice with a reason tied to the community's needs earns credit.
s: Calculation showing the shortfall of Rs 7 lakh
Resource and the two alternative uses named
What is given up if the road is built
One consideration for each choice
A reasoned decision

questions.q: The chapter says 'Human wants are unlimited and keep changing.' Explain how this affects production in an economy, link it to the limits on resources and say why not all wants can be met.
questions.a: Because wants keep changing (bicycle to motorbike to car), people ask for new goods and services, so producers keep making new things. Making them needs resources such as land, labour, capital and technology, which are limited and have alternative uses. Using them for one want gives up others, so choices are needed and not every want can be met.
s: Wants keep changing, with an example
Production responds to new wants
Production uses limited factors of production
Alternative uses mean something is given up
Conclusion: not all wants can be satisfied

questions.q:
Sundarpur Government School has a grant of Rs 60,000. The staff want three things: 100 storybooks at Rs 250 each, a projector for Rs 28,000 and a sports kit for Rs 22,000.
(a) What do all three cost together, and by how much does this exceed the grant?
(b) Which pairs of items can the grant fully pay for, and how much would remain in each case?
(c) Using the chapter's idea, what is given up if the school buys the books and the projector?
(d) Choose one pair to buy and justify the choice, saying what the school loses by it.
questions.a: (a) 25,000 + 28,000 + 22,000 = Rs 75,000, which is Rs 15,000 more than the grant. (b) Books and projector Rs 53,000 leaving Rs 7,000; books and sports kit Rs 47,000 leaving Rs 13,000; projector and sports kit Rs 50,000 leaving Rs 10,000. (c) The sports kit, worth Rs 22,000, is given up; this is the opportunity cost. (d) Any pair is defensible if the loss is stated, e.g. books and kit serve more students directly but give up the projector.
s: (a) Rs 75,000 and the excess of Rs 15,000
(b) The three affordable pairs with leftovers
(c) The sports kit named as the opportunity cost
(d) A reasoned choice stating what is lost

questions.q:
Kaveri Metals has 600 tonnes of steel a month. Each tonne earns a profit of Rs 8,000 if made into refrigerator bodies, Rs 6,500 as medical equipment and Rs 11,000 as aircraft parts. The aircraft buyer will take at most 200 tonnes. A hospital supplier asks for 100 tonnes of medical equipment.
(a) What profit results if all 600 tonnes become refrigerator bodies?
(b) What profit results if 200 tonnes go to aircraft parts and the rest to refrigerators?
(c) How much profit does the firm give up if 100 of the refrigerator tonnes go to the hospital supplier instead?
(d) Should the firm accept the hospital order? Give a justified judgement that weighs profit against other considerations.
questions.a: (a) 600 x 8,000 = Rs 4,800,000. (b) 200 x 11,000 + 400 x 8,000 = Rs 5,400,000. (c) 100 x (8,000 - 6,500) = Rs 150,000 less profit. (d) Either answer is defensible: accepting gives up Rs 1,50,000 of profit but serves hospitals; refusing keeps profit but ignores a need. A clear choice that uses the figures earns full marks.
s: (c) Rs 1,50,000 less profit
(d) A justified decision weighing profit and other considerations

questions.q: On the farmer's table, a move from combination B (25 kg barley, 90 kg wheat) to C (50 kg barley, 70 kg wheat) is being considered. What is the opportunity cost of the extra barley?
questions.a: 20 kg of wheat
o: 20 kg of wheat
25 kg of wheat
70 kg of wheat
25 kg of barley

questions.q: Dinesh has Rs 500. He spends Rs 300 on a cinema ticket and puts nothing towards a cricket bat he was saving for. In the chapter's sense, what is his opportunity cost?
questions.a: The value of the progress towards the bat he gave up
o: The value of the progress towards the bat he gave up
The Rs 300 that he paid for the cinema ticket
The pleasure that he got from watching the film
Every other thing that he could have bought with Rs 500

questions.q: The farmer actually grows 50 kg of barley and 50 kg of wheat. Her table shows that 50 kg of barley can go with 70 kg of wheat. What does her actual output suggest?
questions.a: Her resources are underused, as 20 kg more wheat is possible
o: Her resources are underused, as 20 kg more wheat is possible
She is on the curve, because every point that she can reach lies on it
She needs more land than she has in order to reach this output
Barley has become more valuable to her than wheat has

questions.q: The farmer's curve falls from the top left (A) to the bottom right (E). Which statement best explains the downward slope?
questions.a: Land, water and labour are limited, so more barley means less wheat
o: Land, water and labour are limited, so more barley means less wheat
Wheat becomes cheaper as barley output increases, so she grows less of it
Barley needs less land than wheat, so land is freed up for more wheat
The farmer works fewer hours as she moves along the curve towards E

questions.q:
Match each term with its meaning as used in the farmer's example.
Column A: 1. Opportunity cost; 2. Production Possibility Curve; 3. A point on the curve; 4. Trade-off between barley and wheat
Column B: a. Combinations of goods that can be produced using all available resources; b. The value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen; c. More of one good means less of the other; d. Maximum output from efficient use of resources, avoiding wastage
A district planner draws a curve for two goods, schools and clinics, using the district's full budget. Which use of the curve agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: To see the best combinations and what is sacrificed to get more of one
o: To see the best combinations and what is sacrificed to get more of one
To show that the district can have unlimited schools and unlimited clinics together
To decide the prices of schools and clinics using demand and supply
To prove that the district should always build only schools first

questions.q:
Study the farmer's table of barley and wheat combinations.
I. Every point on the curve shows the maximum output that efficient use of resources can give.
II. Moving from A to E, the farmer's wheat falls at every step while her barley rises.
III. The opportunity cost of growing more barley is the extra barley itself.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I only
II and III only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Combination C (50 kg barley and 70 kg wheat) lies on the farmer's production possibility curve.
Reason (R): Opportunity cost is the value of what is given up when a choice is made.
Choose the correct alternative.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true

questions.q:
Use the farmer's table: moving from C (50 kg barley, 70 kg wheat) to D (75 kg barley, 40 kg wheat).
(a) How much extra barley is grown and how much wheat given up?
(b) How many kg of wheat does each extra kg of barley cost?
questions.a: (a) 25 kg more barley; 70 - 40 = 30 kg less wheat. (b) 30 / 25 = 1.2 kg of wheat per kg of barley.
s: (a) 25 kg barley gained and 30 kg wheat given up
(b) 1.2 kg of wheat per kg of barley

questions.q: True or False: When the farmer grows more barley, the wheat she has to give up is the opportunity cost of that barley. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter defines opportunity cost as the value of what is given up when one alternative is chosen, and the wheat is what she gives up to get more barley.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: opportunity cost is the value of what is given up

questions.q: State what the production possibility curve in the farmer's example shows, and name what each axis measures.
questions.a: It shows the combinations of two goods, barley and wheat, that can be produced with all available resources, and the trade-off between them. The x-axis is barley in kg and the y-axis is wheat in kg.
s: What the curve shows: combinations and the trade-off
Barley on the x-axis and wheat on the y-axis

questions.q:
From A to E on the table, the farmer's barley goes from 0 kg to 100 kg.
(a) How much wheat does she give up over the whole move?
(b) Why can she not have 100 kg of barley and 100 kg of wheat together?
questions.a: (a) Wheat falls from 100 kg to 0, so she gives up 100 kg. (b) Land, water and labour are limited, so the curve shows the most she can produce and 100 kg of each lies beyond it.
s: (a) 100 kg of wheat
(b) Limited resources set the maximum shown by the curve

questions.q: How does understanding opportunity cost improve the quality of an economic decision? Answer with a short example.
questions.a: It makes the decision-maker look at what is given up and compare the alternatives, so choices are made knowingly. Example: a farmer who sees that more barley costs wheat can plan her crop mix.
s: Seeing what is given up and comparing alternatives
A suitable example

questions.q: Rina says, 'On the curve, more barley always means less wheat, so the extra barley is the opportunity cost.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. She is correct that more barley means giving up wheat. She is wrong to call the barley the opportunity cost: the opportunity cost is the wheat given up, the value of what is sacrificed.
s: Verdict: partly right
The correct part: more barley means less wheat
The error: opportunity cost is the wheat given up, not the barley gained

questions.q: The farmer wants 75 kg of barley and 60 kg of wheat. Using her table, show that this cannot be produced and say what the table shows is the most wheat she can have with 75 kg of barley.
questions.a: At 75 kg of barley the table (point D) allows 40 kg of wheat, and 60 kg is more than 40 kg, so the target lies beyond what her resources can give. The most is 40 kg.
s: Locate 75 kg of barley at point D
Compare 60 kg with the 40 kg limit
State that 40 kg is the most wheat

questions.q: A bakery uses one oven for cakes and bread. Write three combinations of cakes and loaves that could form a trade-off curve for one day, and give the opportunity cost of moving from the first to the second combination.
questions.a: Any valid set with cakes rising as loaves fall, e.g. (0 cakes, 80 loaves), (20 cakes, 60 loaves), (40 cakes, 30 loaves); moving from the first to the second gives up 20 loaves for 20 cakes.
s: Three combinations with a downward trade-off
Moving between two named correctly
Opportunity cost stated in loaves given up

questions.q:
Use the farmer's table of barley and wheat (A: 0, 100; B: 25, 90; C: 50, 70; D: 75, 40; E: 100, 0).
(i) Find the wheat given up in each step from A to B, B to C, C to D and D to E.
(ii) Describe the pattern in these numbers.
(iii) The farmer is at C and thinks of moving to D. State the condition under which the move is worth making, and say whether you would advise it.
questions.a: (i) 10 kg, 20 kg, 30 kg and 40 kg of wheat for each 25 kg of barley. (ii) The wheat given up grows with every step, so each extra 25 kg of barley costs more wheat than the one before. (iii) C to D gains 25 kg of barley and loses 30 kg of wheat, so it is worth it only if she values 25 kg of barley more than 30 kg of wheat. Any reasoned advice on this basis earns the mark.
s: Four wheat losses computed
Pattern: the loss rises with each step
C to D: 25 kg gained for 30 kg lost
Condition: value of the barley exceeds the value of the wheat
A reasoned recommendation

questions.q:
A district has a fixed budget. Its combinations of schools and clinics that use it fully are (0 schools, 50 clinics), (10, 44), (20, 32), (30, 16) and (40, 0).
(i) Find the clinics given up for each extra 10 schools.
(ii) Explain how this resembles the farmer's curve.
(iii) Explain how a planner can use such a curve in decision-making, and why a combination of 20 schools and 20 clinics would not be a good plan.
questions.a: (i) 6, 12, 16 and 16 clinics given up. (ii) It is a trade-off curve sloping downward, because the budget is limited: more of one means less of the other, and the clinics given up are the opportunity cost of schools. (iii) The planner sees the best combinations and what each costs. 20 schools and 20 clinics falls inside the curve, since 20 schools can go with 32 clinics, so the budget is not being used fully.
s: Four losses computed
Downward trade-off from limited resources
Clinics given up named as opportunity cost
The planning use of the curve
20 and 20 identified as wasteful because 32 clinics are possible

questions.q:
Lakshmi farms the land of the chapter's table. This season barley sells at Rs 30 per kg and wheat at Rs 25 per kg. Her family needs 40 kg of wheat for the year. She can choose any one of the five combinations in the table: A (0 kg barley, 100 kg wheat), B (25, 90), C (50, 70), D (75, 40) or E (100, 0).
(a) Work out the sale value of each combination.
(b) Which combinations meet her family's wheat need, and which of these earn the most?
(c) What does she give up, in kg and in rupees, by moving from C to D?
(d) Choose between the best combinations and justify your choice using more than the sale value.
questions.a: (a) A Rs 2,500; B Rs 3,000; C Rs 3,250; D Rs 3,250; E Rs 3,000. (b) A, B, C and D leave at least 40 kg of wheat; E does not. C and D earn the most, Rs 3,250 each. (c) She gives up 30 kg of wheat (Rs 750) to gain 25 kg of barley (Rs 750). (d) C and D tie on money, so the choice rests on other things: C leaves 30 kg of wheat beyond her family's need, while D puts all spare effort into barley. Either is defensible with a clear reason.
s: (a) Sale values of all five combinations
(b) Combinations meeting the need and the top earners
(c) 30 kg of wheat, Rs 750, against 25 kg of barley, Rs 750
(d) A reasoned choice between equal earners

questions.q:
Ananya has 5 free hours each evening. A tuition session takes 2 hours and cricket practice is counted in whole hours. She cannot go beyond 5 hours.
(a) For 0, 1 and 2 tuition sessions, what is the most cricket practice she can fit in?
(b) What is the opportunity cost, in hours of cricket, of one tuition session?
(c) Say whether each plan is on her limit, inside it or impossible: 2 sessions and 2 hours of cricket; 1 session and 2 hours of cricket; 0 sessions and 5 hours of cricket.
(d) Her exam is in ten days and the team trial is next week. Choose between 1 session with 3 hours of cricket and 2 sessions with 1 hour of cricket, and justify.
questions.a: (a) 5, 3 and 1 hours. (b) 2 hours of cricket. (c) 2 sessions and 2 hours need 6 hours, so impossible; 1 session and 2 hours need 4 hours, leaving 1 hour unused, so inside her limit; 0 sessions and 5 hours use exactly 5 hours, so on the limit. (d) Either is defensible with reasons: the first balances both, the second favours exam preparation at the cost of two hours of practice.
s: (a) 5, 3 and 1 hours
(b) 2 hours of cricket per session
(c) Impossible, inside and on the limit correctly assigned
(d) A justified choice that names what is given up

questions.q: A newspaper explains economics to children as 'running a big household with limited means'. Which part of the word's Greek origin supports this description?
questions.a: Oikos means household and nemein means management
o: Oikos means household and nemein means management
Oikos means market and nemein means trading
Oikos means money and nemein means counting
Oikos means nation and nemein means ruling

questions.q: Which pairing of an economic entity with an activity matches the chapter?
questions.a: Governments use revenue from taxation to plan spending on infrastructure and welfare
o: Governments use revenue from taxation to plan spending on infrastructure and welfare
Families study market trends and new innovations to maximise profits
Enterprises prepare the annual Economic Survey for Parliament
Financial institutions decide how a household divides its income between essentials and savings

questions.q: Manoj is an economist who advises a state government on how much to tax and how much to spend on welfare. Which area of the economist's work, as listed in the chapter, is this?
questions.a: Policy-making
o: Policy-making
Finance
Research and education
Business consulting

questions.q: A reporter wants an annual review of how agriculture, industry and services performed last year, along with the challenges ahead. Which source suits her best?
questions.a: The Economic Survey of the Ministry of Finance
o: The Economic Survey of the Ministry of Finance
A company's own yearly financial statements
A school's annual report on its results
A household's monthly budget for its expenses

questions.q: A student says, 'Economics is about households only, so it has nothing to say about nations.' Which idea from the chapter answers her best?
questions.a: Nations too must plan the use of limited resources against unlimited wants
o: Nations too must plan the use of limited resources against unlimited wants
Nations have unlimited resources, so they do not need to plan their use at all
Households and nations use the same budget, so they are really one entity
Only governments, and never families, have to take economic decisions

questions.q: A family earns Rs 20,000 in a month, spends Rs 11,000 on essential items and Rs 4,000 on non-essential items, and saves the rest. The amount saved, in rupees, is ___.

Read the statements about economists and the Economic Survey.
I. The Economic Survey is prepared by the Planning Commission and is presented after the Union Budget.
II. Economists use data from government reports such as economic surveys and from the financial statements of companies.
III. Economics explains how consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions interact in an economy.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I only
I and II only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Economics deals only with the money that individuals earn.
Reason (R): Economics explains how consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions interact in an economy.
Choose the correct alternative.
questions.a: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
o: The Assertion is false but the Reason is true
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false

questions.q:
A family's income is Rs 24,000 a month. It spends Rs 15,600 on essential items and Rs 5,400 on non-essential items and saves the rest.
(a) How much is saved, and what percentage of income is that?
(b) If income fell and the family had to cut one of the three heads first, which would the chapter's classification suggest, and why?
questions.a: (a) 24,000 - 15,600 - 5,400 = Rs 3,000, which is 12.5 per cent of income. (b) Non-essential items, because essentials such as food, medicines and school supplies are needed, while non-essentials such as jewellery and entertainment are not.
s: (a) Rs 3,000 and 12.5 per cent
(b) Non-essentials, with the reason from the classification

questions.q: True or False: The Economic Survey is presented in Parliament after the Union Budget, to review how the Budget worked. Correct it if it is wrong.
questions.a: False. The Economic Survey is presented in Parliament before the Union Budget, and it acts as a blueprint for the upcoming Budget.
s: Verdict: false
Correction: presented before the Budget and used as its blueprint

questions.q: Differentiate between 'data' and a 'survey' as the chapter defines them.
questions.a: Data are facts and statistics collected together for reference or analysis; a survey is a systematic method for collecting and analysing data about the economic conditions and behaviour of populations.
s: Data defined as facts and statistics for reference or analysis
Survey defined as a systematic method of collecting and analysing data

questions.q:
(a) What does the Economic Survey let a citizen judge about the Indian economy?
(b) Why does it help the government when it prepares the Union Budget?
questions.a: (a) How the economy performed in the past year across sectors such as agriculture, industry and services, with future challenges and opportunities, explained clearly with data. (b) It provides insights for policymakers and acts as a blueprint for the upcoming Budget.
s: (a) Past-year performance and challenges explained with data
(b) Insights for policymakers, a blueprint for the Budget

questions.q: The chapter says good decisions rely on data and analysis, not guesswork. Give one example of how an enterprise uses this idea.
questions.a: An enterprise studies market trends and new innovations to serve customers better and maximise profits, e.g. a snack maker checks past sales before deciding how many packets to make.
s: Data and analysis rather than guesswork
A suitable example of an enterprise using market data

questions.q: Ishaan says, 'The Economic Survey reviews last year's performance and also discusses future challenges, so it helps policymakers decide the next steps.' Is he right?
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the Survey reviews the past year across sectors and also discusses future challenges and opportunities, which helps people see how the economy is performing and what steps the government may take.
s: Verdict: he is right
Past-year review across sectors
Future challenges used to decide the steps to take

questions.q: Describe a situation, of your own, in which an economist working in business consulting or finance uses data to give advice. Name the area of work and the data used.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. a consultant studies a firm's monthly sales data and costs to help it plan growth (business consulting), or an adviser compares company financial statements to tell an investor where to invest (finance).
s: A believable situation
The area of work named correctly
The data used identified

questions.q: Using one family example and one government example from the chapter, explain why economics can be called 'household management' for a nation.
questions.a: A family divides money among essentials, non-essentials and savings; a government uses revenue from taxation to plan spending on infrastructure and welfare. Both have limited resources and unlimited wants, so both must plan their use, which is why economics is household management at the level of a nation.
s: Family example of dividing limited money
Government example of planning spending from tax revenue
Link: both manage limited resources

questions.q:
Two shopkeepers each stock 300 packets of a snack every week. One of them has noted last four weeks' sales (240, 260, 250 and 270 packets); the other guesses.
(i) Find the average weekly sales.
(ii) How many packets would a 300-packet stock leave unsold in an average week?
(iii) Explain, with this example, the chapter's view that good decisions rely on data and analysis.
(iv) Name one limit on how far past sales can guide the next decision.
questions.a: (i) (240 + 260 + 250 + 270) / 4 = 255 packets. (ii) 300 - 255 = 45 packets. (iii) The first shopkeeper can plan stock near 255 from evidence, while the guesser risks waste; the chapter says decisions need data and analysis, not guesswork. (iv) Past sales may not repeat if tastes or markets change, so data must be reliable and current.
s: Average 255
45 packets unsold
Data-based stocking compared with guesswork
Link to the chapter's view
A reasoned limit on past data

questions.q: Describe what the Economic Survey contains, say who is helped by it and how, and explain how it connects to the Union Budget.
questions.a: The Survey is an annual document prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented in Parliament before the Union Budget. It reviews the economy's performance in the past year, analyses sectors such as agriculture, industry and services and areas such as employment, inflation, education, health and infrastructure, and discusses future challenges. Citizens are helped because it explains economic data clearly; policymakers are helped with insights for decisions. It works as a blueprint for the upcoming Budget.
s: Prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented in Parliament before the Budget
Reviews past-year performance and sectors
Discusses future challenges and opportunities
Who gains: citizens and policymakers
Blueprint for the Union Budget

questions.q:
The Rampur municipality has Rs 12 crore of tax revenue. It is considering a water pipeline (Rs 5.5 crore), school repairs (Rs 4 crore) and street lights (Rs 3.5 crore). A survey of 2,000 households found that 840 have no piped water, 300 live in lanes without street lights and 460 have a child in a school building reported unsafe.
(a) What percentage of the surveyed households is affected by each problem?
(b) By how much do the three projects exceed the revenue?
(c) Which pair of projects uses the revenue best without exceeding it, and how much is left?
(d) Decide how the municipality should use its revenue, and justify with the survey.
questions.a: (a) Water 42 per cent; lights 15 per cent; unsafe schools 23 per cent. (b) 5.5 + 4 + 3.5 = Rs 13.0 crore, Rs 1 crore above the revenue. (c) The pipeline and the school repairs cost Rs 9.5 crore, leaving Rs 2.5 crore. (d) A defensible choice is the pipeline and schools, since they affect the most households, then deciding what to do with Rs 2.5 crore; another answer is fine if it uses the survey and states what is given up.
s: (a) 42, 15 and 23 per cent
(b) Rs 1 crore more than the revenue
(c) Pipeline plus school repairs, Rs 2.5 crore left
(d) A decision based on survey data that names what is given up

questions.q:
Sunrise Beverages sold the following bottles in four months. Mango: 400, 460, 530, 610. Orange: 500, 490, 480, 470. The firm can make at most 1,000 bottles of the two flavours together each month.
(a) Find the average monthly sale of each flavour.
(b) Find the percentage change from the first month to the fourth for each flavour.
(c) Why would the averages alone give the firm a misleading picture?
(d) The owner must decide where to put the extra machine time next month. Advise her, using the chapter's idea on data, and mention one risk of your advice.
questions.a: (a) Mango 500 bottles; orange 485 bottles. (b) Mango +52.5 per cent; orange -6.0 per cent. (c) The averages are almost equal, but the trends run in opposite directions, so averages hide that mango is growing and orange is slipping. (d) Giving more machine time to mango fits the trend; the risk is that the rise may not continue. An answer for keeping some orange production is acceptable if it is supported by the data.
s: (b) +52.5 per cent and -6 per cent
(c) Averages hide opposite trends
(d) Advice from the data with a stated risk

questions.q: A garment manufacturer finds that machines have become much cheaper while skilled workers have become costly and scarce. According to the chapter, what is she likely to do?
questions.a: Shift towards machine-based, capital-intensive production
o: Shift towards machine-based, capital-intensive production
Add more workers, because costly labour is more efficient
Stop producing garments until machines become costly again
Ask the government to fix the price of every garment

questions.q: A boutique makes bridal wear stitched to each customer's measurements and design. Which method of production does the chapter's reasoning favour for it?
questions.a: Skilled labour, since customised clothes need skilled workers
o: Skilled labour, since customised clothes need skilled workers
Fully automated machines, since each piece is mass-produced in large numbers
Machines only, since labour laws forbid hand work in any garment unit
Unskilled labour, since the product is standard and needs no particular skill

questions.q: A shoe company wants to serve factory workers who need affordable and durable footwear. Which choice of material fits the chapter?
questions.a: Rubber or synthetic material
o: Rubber or synthetic material
Polished leather
Special lightweight sports soles for grip and flexibility
Imported fabric chosen for formal appearance

questions.q: A village panchayat encourages every farmer to grow sugarcane because it yields high profits. In the chapter's example, what is the opportunity cost of this choice?
questions.a: The forgone gains from saved water and better soil
o: The forgone gains from saved water and better soil
The profits that the sugar industry earns from the cane crop
The seeds and fertiliser that are used to grow the sugarcane
The price that the millets would have fetched in the market

questions.q: A bakery replaces hand-kneading with a dough-mixing machine to cut costs. Which of the three key economic questions is it answering?
questions.a: How to produce
o: How to produce
What to produce
For whom to produce
How to remove scarcity altogether

questions.q:
Match each concept with the example the chapter uses for it.
Column A: 1. Labour-intensive production; 2. Capital-intensive production; 3. For whom to produce; 4. What to produce
Column B: a. Steel and automobile manufacturing; b. Choosing between sugarcane and paddy or millets and pulses; c. Agriculture and handicrafts; d. School shoes for students and sports shoes for athletes

Read the statements about how to produce.
I. Steel and automobile manufacturing depend more on labour than on machinery.
II. The availability of factors of production and their relative cost help decide how an enterprise produces.
III. Laws and regulations in a country have no effect on the choice of production method.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only
o: II only
I and II only
II and III only
All three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's example, the opportunity cost of producing sugarcane is the gains forgone from saved water and improved soil health.
Reason (R): Sugarcane yields lower profits than millets and pulses.
Choose the correct alternative.
questions.a: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
o: The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true

questions.q:
A hand-stitching unit has 40 workers who stitch 30 shirts a day each. A machine line makes the same total with 8 workers.
(a) Find the output per worker in each method.
(b) Name the method that is capital-intensive, and say what it uses more of.
questions.a: (a) Hand unit: 40 x 30 = 1,200 shirts, 30 per worker; machine line: 1,200 / 8 = 150 per worker. (b) The machine line is capital-intensive, as it uses more machines and technology and fewer workers.
s: (a) 30 and 150 shirts per worker
(b) Machine line named, using more machines and technology

questions.q: True or False: Producers decide 'for whom to produce' by studying what consumers like, how much money they have and how much demand there is. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says producers analyse these things before deciding what to make, so that limited resources are used well and not wasted.
s: Verdict: true
Reason: it makes sure limited resources are used well and not wasted

questions.q: Differentiate between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production, giving one example of each from the chapter.
questions.a: Labour-intensive production uses more workers and less machinery (agriculture and handicrafts); capital-intensive production uses more machines and technology and fewer workers (steel or automobile manufacturing).
s: The two methods differentiated
One example of each

questions.q:
(a) Name two factors the chapter says affect a firm's choice of production technique.
(b) A garment manufacturer's machines become affordable. What does the chapter say she may do?
questions.a: (a) Any two: cost of capital, level of technology, nature of the product, availability and relative cost of factors, laws and regulations. (b) She may shift to automation.
s: (a) Two valid factors
(b) Shift to automation

questions.q: Why do shoe makers produce school shoes, office shoes, sports shoes and casual shoes instead of one type for everyone? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: People have different needs, income levels, tastes and lifestyles, so producers pick the group they want to serve. This also helps limited resources to be used well and not wasted.
s: Different needs, incomes, tastes and lifestyles
Limited resources used well, not wasted

questions.q: Vikram says, 'A farmer should always grow sugarcane because it gives high profits and nothing is lost by choosing it.' Examine his claim.
questions.a: No. Sugarcane does give high profits and supports industries such as sugar, but something is lost: the gains from saved water and improved soil health that millets and pulses offer. The choice is a trade-off between short-term gains and long-term sustainability.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
What sugarcane does gain
What is lost: the forgone water and soil health benefits

questions.q: Meera says, 'A firm may use machines for its mass-produced garments and skilled workers for its customised ones, and the chapter supports both.' Is she right?
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says customised or designer clothes require skilled labour, while mass-produced garments are better suited for machines, so using both methods for different products agrees with it.
s: Verdict: she is right
Customised clothes need skilled labour
Mass-produced garments suit machines

questions.q: Design a footwear product for one group of buyers of your own choice. Name the group, give two features and the material, in line with the chapter's examples.
questions.a: Any valid answer, e.g. a rainy-day sandal for daily wear: comfortable and affordable (casual shoes or slippers), made of rubber or synthetic material for durability.
s: A buyer group identified
Two features suited to the group
A suitable material linked to the group

questions.q:
A village has 100 acres. Each acre of sugarcane earns Rs 80,000 and needs 10 units of water; each acre of millets earns Rs 50,000 and needs 4 units. The village has 640 units of water and plants every acre with one of the two crops.
(i) What is the most acres of sugarcane it can plant?
(ii) Compare the earnings of that plan with an all-millets plan.
(iii) How much water does the all-millets plan save compared with the plan in (i)?
(iv) Using the chapter, say what the village gives up by planting that much sugarcane, and recommend a plan.
questions.a: (i) If x acres are sugarcane: 10x + 4(100-x) <= 640, so x <= 40 acres. (ii) 40 x 80,000 + 60 x 50,000 = Rs 6,200,000; all millets earn 100 x 50,000 = Rs 5,000,000. (iii) The all-millets plan uses 400 units against 640, saving 240 units. (iv) The village gives up the saved water and better soil health that millets and pulses bring, for Rs 12,00,000 more now. A reasoned recommendation, with the short-term gain against long-term sustainability trade-off, earns the mark.
s: Maximum sugarcane of 40 acres
Earnings Rs 62,00,000 against Rs 50,00,000
240 units of water saved
What is given up, in the chapter's terms
A reasoned recommendation

questions.q: A footwear firm serves four groups of buyers. Explain how the 'for whom to produce' decision shapes its products for each group, how it affects the materials used, and why the firm studies buyers before deciding.
questions.a: School shoes are simple, durable and affordable for students; office shoes focus on comfort, formal appearance and quality for working professionals; sports shoes use special rubber soles and light materials for grip, flexibility and support; casual shoes or slippers are comfortable and affordable for daily use. Leather is aimed at office-goers and high-income customers, while rubber or synthetic shoes suit sports players, factory workers or people needing affordable and durable footwear. The firm analyses likes, incomes and demand so that limited resources are used well and not wasted.
s: Features of at least two groups' shoes
Material linked to the group
Study of likes, income and demand
Purpose: limited resources not wasted

questions.q:
Jaya Garments pays each worker Rs 600 a day. Method 1: 40 workers stitch 1,200 shirts a day by hand. Method 2: a machine line needs 8 workers and costs Rs 9,000 a day to rent and run, and also makes 1,200 shirts a day.
(a) What is the daily cost of each method?
(b) What is the cost per shirt in each?
(c) At what daily wage would the two methods cost the same?
(d) The 40 workers have been with the firm for years. Decide which method Jaya should use, and justify using the chapter's factors.
questions.a: (a) Hand: 40 x 600 = Rs 24,000; machine: 8 x 600 + 9,000 = Rs 13,800. (b) Rs 20 and Rs 11.5 per shirt. (c) 40w = 8w + 9,000 gives w = Rs 281.25. (d) At Rs 600 the machine line is cheaper, but the choice also depends on the labour laws, the cost of capital and the type of order. Either decision is defensible if the factors are weighed and the loss is stated.
s: (b) Rs 20 and Rs 11.5
(d) A decision weighing the chapter's factors

questions.q:
Strides Footwear has Rs 12 lakh to set up one new line. The cost of producing a pair, profit per pair and monthly demand are: school shoes (Rs 300, Rs 150, 4,000 pairs); office shoes (Rs 900, Rs 400, 1,200 pairs); sports shoes (Rs 700, Rs 350, 1,500 pairs); casual shoes (Rs 150, Rs 90, 6,000 pairs). It plans to meet the full monthly demand of the line it picks.
(a) What money would each line need and what monthly profit would it earn?
(b) Find the profit earned per rupee spent on each line.
(c) How much of the Rs 12 lakh stays unused under the casual shoes line?
(d) Decide which group to serve and justify, naming what the firm gives up.
questions.a: (a) School Rs 12,00,000 and Rs 6,00,000; office Rs 10,80,000 and Rs 4,80,000; sports Rs 10,50,000 and Rs 5,25,000; casual Rs 9,00,000 and Rs 5,40,000. (b) 0.50, 0.44, 0.50 and 0.60. (c) 12,00,000 - 9,00,000 = Rs 3,00,000. (d) School shoes give the most profit and use all the money; casual shoes give the best return per rupee but leave Rs 3 lakh unused. Either choice is acceptable if the loss is named.
s: (a) Money needed and profit for all four lines
(b) Profit per rupee for each
(d) A justified decision stating what is given up

questions.q: In a country, a central authority sets output targets for factories and enterprises need strict permits and licences to produce. What result does the chapter say this is likely to have?
questions.a: Little motivation for enterprises to improve quality or innovate
o: Little motivation for enterprises to improve quality or innovate
Many producers compete with each other, so prices fall and quality rises
Prices and output come to be decided mainly by demand and supply
The government steps back and acts only as a referee to the market

questions.q: In a market economy a new bakery opens in a lane that already has five bakeries. What effect does the chapter expect from this?
questions.a: Competition encourages better quality, lower prices and innovation
o: Competition encourages better quality, lower prices and innovation
The government fixes the price of every loaf
A central authority issues production targets to each bakery
The new bakery cannot open without a licence from the planning authority

questions.q: The chapter compares the government in a market economy to a referee in a football match. Which action fits that role?
questions.a: Ensuring safety and law and order without controlling prices
o: Ensuring safety and law and order without controlling prices
Setting the price at which rice is to be sold in every shop
Deciding how many cars each of the factories has to build
Owning and running all the banks, roads and other businesses

questions.q: A history project describes India's economy in the decades after Independence. Which description agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: A state-led approach like a planned economy, with licences and a dominant public sector
o: A state-led approach like a planned economy, with licences and a dominant public sector
A market economy in which private firms dominated banking and transport, with no controls on them
A mixed economy in which the government stayed out of production and left licences alone
A planned economy that banned all private trade and every import into the country

questions.q:
Match each group of countries or goods with the term the chapter uses for it.
Column A: 1. Former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba; 2. USA, Japan and Hong Kong; 3. India after 1991, China after 1978, Germany and Sweden; 4. Parks, roads, police services and street lights
Column B: a. Mixed economies; b. Public goods; c. Planned economies; d. Market economies

In a country, rules keep competition fair, consumers are protected and the state provides parks and roads, while businesses chase profit. Because both government and private firms shape choices, it is called a ___ economy.
questions.a: mixed

questions.q:
Read the statements about economic systems.
I. In a market economy the ownership of factories, shops and land largely rests with individuals and private companies.
II. In a planned economy strict permits and licences restrict competition among private enterprises.
III. Even market economies like the USA and Singapore have significant government involvement in the market.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three
o: All three
I only
I and II only
II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a planned economy, enterprises have little motivation to improve quality or innovate.
Reason (R): Strict permits and licences prevent many enterprises from operating, which restricts competition.
Choose the correct alternative.
questions.a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
o: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
The Assertion is true but the Reason is false
The Assertion is false but the Reason is true

questions.q:
In the country of Zora, a central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce, and the government owns most land, factories, banks and transport.
(a) Name the system and one country from the chapter that follows it.
(b) Which of the three key questions does the authority settle in this system?
questions.a: (a) A planned economy; examples are the former Soviet Union, North Korea and Cuba. (b) All three: what to produce, how to produce and for whom, along with the prices at which goods are available.
s: (a) Planned economy with an example country
(b) The authority settles all three key questions

questions.q: True or False: In a market economy the government plays no role at all. Give the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says governments play an important role even in market economies: they ensure safety and law and order and provide public goods and infrastructure, though they do not control prices or production.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: the government still keeps law and order and provides public goods

questions.q: Differentiate between a planned economy and a market economy on who owns resources and who makes the major decisions.
questions.a: In a planned economy the government owns most resources and a central authority makes the major decisions. In a market economy ownership rests largely with private individuals and companies, and demand and supply decide what, how and how much to produce.
s: Planned: government ownership, central authority decides
Market: private ownership, demand and supply decide

questions.q:
(a) State two changes that the reforms of the early 1990s brought to India's economy.
(b) Did the reforms make India a purely market economy? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Any two: they reduced excessive regulations, encouraged private enterprise, opened the economy to global trade and investment, increased competition. (b) No. They moved India gradually towards a market-oriented system while still keeping an important role for the government, so it is a mixed economy.
s: (a) Two valid changes
(b) No, the government still has an important role

questions.q: What are public goods? Give two examples and say why they are linked to the government's role in an economy.
questions.a: Public goods are available to all without anyone being excluded, and use by some does not stop others using them; examples are parks and roads. The chapter links them to the government's role of providing public goods and physical infrastructure.
s: Meaning of public goods with two examples
Linked to the government's role

questions.q: Karan says, 'In a market economy, private ownership and competition improve quality, lower prices and encourage innovation, so the government need do nothing.' How far is he right?
questions.a: Partly right. The first part agrees with the chapter: many producers encourage better quality, lower prices and innovation. He is wrong that the government does nothing: it acts like a referee, ensuring safety and law and order, and provides public goods.
s: Verdict: partly right
The correct part about private ownership and competition
The error: the government still acts as referee and provides public goods

questions.q: Sana says, 'After the reforms of 1991 the government no longer matters in India, which is now run purely by the market.' Examine her claim.
questions.a: No. The reforms reduced excessive regulation, encouraged private enterprise and opened up trade, but the chapter says they shifted India towards a more market-oriented system while still retaining an important role for the government, with large public sector companies still significant. India is a mixed economy.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
What the reforms changed
The government's role was retained, so India is mixed

questions.q: Describe an imaginary country as a mixed economy. Give three features, at least one from the market side and one from the government side.
questions.a: Any valid description, e.g. private firms compete and own factories (market side), the government enforces fair competition rules and protects consumers, and runs welfare programmes and public goods such as roads (government side).
s: A market-side feature
A government-side feature
A third feature consistent with a mixed economy

questions.q: 'Pure economic systems rarely exist.' Examine this statement. Discuss a limit of the planned and market systems as the chapter describes them, and explain why a mixed economy is often seen as a practical approach.
questions.a: In a planned economy the government owns most resources, strict permits restrict competition, and enterprises have little motivation to improve quality or innovate. In a market economy the government acts as referee and still provides public goods, and even the USA and Singapore have significant government involvement, so a pure market is rare. Almost all economies are mixed, as in India after 1991, China, Germany and Sweden. A mixed economy combines private enterprise, competition and innovation with government rules, consumer protection, welfare and public goods. Any reasoned view along these lines earns credit.
s: A limit of the planned system with detail
Why a pure market economy is rare
Almost all economies are mixed, with examples
What the mixed economy combines
A reasoned judgement about practicality

questions.q: A country must decide how many tractors to produce, by what method and for whom. Describe how the decision would be made in a planned, a market and a mixed economy, and mention one strength or weakness of each approach from the chapter.
questions.a: Planned: a central authority decides the number, method and who gets them, at what prices; enterprises follow its targets; weakness is little motivation to innovate. Market: demand and supply decide, private firms choose the number and method, many producers encourage better quality and lower prices; the government acts as referee. Mixed: private firms and the government both play roles, with the government setting fair rules and providing public goods while private enterprise competes.
s: Planned: central authority decides
Market: demand and supply and private firms decide
Mixed: both play roles
One strength or weakness from the chapter
All three key questions covered

questions.q:
In the fictional country of Veloria, scooters were made by one licensed state firm: 50,000 a year at Rs 40,000 each. After reforms that cut licensing and allowed private firms, the state firm made 20,000 scooters and three private firms made 25,000 each, and the price fell to Rs 32,000.
(a) By what percentage did total output change?
(b) By what percentage did the price change, and what share of the output does the state firm now make?
(c) Which of the chapter's reasons explains why the price fell and output rose?
(d) The state firm employs 8,000 workers who may lose jobs as its share falls. Decide whether the government should shield the firm with new licence limits on private firms, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Output rose from 50,000 to 95,000, a rise of 90 per cent. (b) The price fell 20 per cent; the state firm makes 21.1 per cent of the output. (c) More producers compete, which encourages lower prices, better quality and innovation. (d) Either decision can be defended: shielding protects jobs but restores restrictions on competition; not shielding keeps the benefits for buyers but risks jobs. A reasoned choice naming the loss earns full marks.
s: (a) 90 per cent rise
(b) 20 per cent fall and about 21.1 per cent share
(c) Competition among many producers
(d) A reasoned decision naming what is given up

questions.q:
In the market town of Sundar Bazaar, 500 households each buy one private water tanker every week. In a dry spell the price rises from Rs 800 to Rs 1,400. The forecast says the spell may last 3 to 6 months (take 4 weeks in a month). The council can either build a public water point for Rs 60 lakh, or do nothing and let the market work.
(a) How much extra does one household pay in a month?
(b) What is the extra monthly cost to all 500 households together?
(c) For how many months of dry spell does the extra cost equal the Rs 60 lakh?
(d) Using the chapter's idea of the government's role, advise the council, and say what your advice risks.
questions.a: (a) 4 x (1,400 - 800) = Rs 2,400. (b) 500 x 2,400 = Rs 1,200,000. (c) 60,00,000 / 12,00,000 = 5 months. (d) For a spell of 3 months the extra cost is Rs 36 lakh, below the cost of the water point; for 6 months it is Rs 72 lakh, above it. Providing a public good is part of the government's role, while a market economy lets prices move; either answer is defensible if it names the risk, such as a costly point if the spell is short.
s: (c) 5 months
(d) Advice linked to the government's role with a stated risk
